| [THEORY-025](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-025.md) v2 | Neither utility information nor resource holdings, alone or together, can register claims that arise from how differently people convert resources into what they can do and be: equal resources leave unequal capabilities, and utility adapts to deprivation | Sen (1979), [LIT-289](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-289.md), first-hand: a contented disabled person has no marginal-utility claim, no total-utility deficit and no primary-goods deficit, yet an evident claim. The negative thesis rests on one case and a shared intuition, and Sen says it stands without his positive proposal. The resourcist reply (Pogge) is not held, and the claim does not say capabilities are the right replacement. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-027](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-027.md) v2 | Two individually decisive people, weak Pareto and an unrestricted domain cannot all hold, even when choice need only yield a best element; unlike Arrow's theorem, the conflict is not removed by interpersonal comparability | Sen (1970), [LIT-285](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-285.md): no social decision function satisfies U, weak Pareto and minimal liberalism. The proof was checked in this record, including the unproved one-way strengthening. Whether pairwise decisiveness is what liberty is remains open, and the record reads the rights-as-game-forms literature only through Sen's reply to it. | Active |
| [THEORY-029](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-029.md) v7 | A higher-order attitude cannot make a motive the agent's own by its order alone: any attitude specified without presupposing the agent's participation can itself be disowned, and any specified to include it presupposes what it was meant to explain | Velleman (1992), [LIT-295](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-295.md): every candidate for the agent's standpoint in a hierarchical account (second-order desire, Watsonian value, decisive commitment) is either disownable or question-begging. Buss & Westlund ([LIT-296](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-296.md)) state the regress as their own argument; McKenna & Coates ([LIT-291](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-291.md)) and Dryden ([LIT-297](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-297.md)) credit it to Watson 1975, which the record has not read. Frankfurt's own 2004 lectures ([LIT-293](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-293.md)) never address it. The dilemma is argued by examples, not proved, and it does not show that higher-order structure is irrelevant to agency. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-040](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-040.md) v6 | A condition on free agency stated only in present psychological structure is met by a manipulated agent, so the account must count that agent free or add a historical condition, and no historical condition in the record's readings is shown to escape | McKenna & Coates, [LIT-291](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-291.md): every "mesh" compatibilism can be installed by a manipulator, and Frankfurt is quoted (2002, second-hand) accepting that a manipulated character leaves a person responsible. Dryden ([LIT-297](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-297.md)) and Buss & Westlund ([LIT-296](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-296.md)) make the same point against hierarchical autonomy. Historical supplements are reported to face "loading-in" and a circularity worry; neither is argued in full in the record. The claim says what the account must choose between, not which choice is wrong. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-075](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-075.md) | Obligation is the reflective rejection of what would violate the agent's practical identity, and moral obligation follows only because valuing any practical identity commits the agent to valuing her humanity | Korsgaard (1992), [LIT-564](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-564.md): because human consciousness is reflective, an agent must act on reasons, and so must identify with some law, a "practical identity": "a description under which you value yourself". "Your reasons express your identity, your nature; your obligations spring from what that identity forbids." Obligation is "the reflective rejection of a threat to your identity", unconditional where violation would be worse than death. Identities are a "jumble" and differ across social worlds, so this much yields no morality. Moral obligation enters because valuing any identity requires valuing one's humanity, the source of all one's reasons. "The Normative Constitution of Agency" ([LIT-587](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-587.md)) later makes practical identity the content of maxims chosen under the formal norms. Argued, with the key steps flagged by their author as sketchy; the commentaries and reply are unread. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-118](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-118.md) | Praiseworthiness is compatible with being psychologically determined by good reasons, but blameworthiness requires that the agent could have done otherwise, that is, could have acted on the right reasons | Susan Wolf's asymmetry thesis, reported second-hand: the primary texts are unread. McKenna and Coates ([LIT-291](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-291.md), §4.3), citing "Asymmetrical Freedom" and Freedom Within Reason pp. 79–81, report that for Wolf praiseworthy conduct does not require the freedom to do otherwise and blameworthy conduct does. An agent determined to act in accord with the True and the Good loses nothing by lacking the ability to act irrationally; an agent who acts against it and cannot act in accord with it cannot reasonably be blamed. In Fischer's terms, only blame needs regulative control. Wolf holds that the ability needs only the falsity of psychological, not physical, determinism. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-119](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-119.md) v2 | An agent can be morally responsible for what she did although she could not have done otherwise, when what made the action unavoidable played no part in bringing it about, so the principle of alternate possibilities is false | Frankfurt (1969, [LIT-694](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-694.md), read): Black stands ready to make Jones4 act as he wants and never needs to, so Jones4 could not have done otherwise and is as responsible, for blame or praise, as without Black. A fact that plays no part in bringing an action about cannot excuse it. The 1971 willing addict ([LIT-692](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-692.md), read) is a second route. Robb's SEP entry ([LIT-294](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-294.md)) gives the standard objections: the dilemma defence from the prior sign, flickers of freedom, general abilities, and the case's oddity. None is settled, and the record has read the replies only in survey. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-120](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-120.md) v2 | A motive is the agent's own, and she acts of her own free will, when she identifies with it, and that is all the freedom moral responsibility requires: identification is the conformity of the effective desire to a decisive higher-order volition (1971), and later wholehearted acceptance with no conflict at any higher order | Frankfurt's hierarchical, or endorsement, account, from his own texts: the 1971 paper ([LIT-692](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-692.md), read) and the 2004 Tanner Lectures ([LIT-293](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-293.md), read). A person's will is the desire that moves him to act; he identifies with a desire by wanting it to be his will, decisively, and he acts of his own free will when the will that moves him is the will he wants. In 2004 the condition is "volitional unanimity" with no conflict "at any higher order", and identification is "willing acceptance", which may be resigned. Acting of one's own free will is what responsibility requires, and alternatives and history are irrelevant. The 1987 and 1992 revisions are held only by report. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-121](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-121.md) v5 | Moral responsibility requires guidance control, moderate reasons-responsiveness of the agent's own actual-sequence mechanism, and not regulative control over alternative possibilities, so responsibility is compatible with causal determinism | Fischer and Ravizza, in their own précis ([LIT-728](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-728.md), read): moral responsibility requires guidance control, not regulative control over alternatives. Guidance control is acting from a mechanism one has made one's own by taking responsibility for it, which is moderately reasons-responsive: regularly receptive to reasons, some moral, and at least weakly reactive. Fischer's 1987 paper ([LIT-687](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-687.md), read) is the weak-responsiveness origin. The view is compatible with causal determinism. | Active |
| [THEORY-122](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-122.md) | Moral responsibility requires the normative competence to recognise and act on the True and the Good, which identification with one's own motives does not supply | Susan Wolf's Reason View, reported second-hand: the primary texts are unread. McKenna and Coates ([LIT-291](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-291.md), §4.3) report that for Wolf free will is the ability to act in accord with the True and the Good, an anchor outside the agent's psychology. Talbert ([LIT-691](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-691.md), §§3.1.1, 3.2) reports her case against deep-self or Real Self views and the JoJo case: JoJo identifies wholly with the cruel values his father raised him in, yet is not responsible, because he cannot appreciate that they are wrong. The claim is a necessary condition. It does not by itself say whether the ability must include being able to do otherwise; that is [THEORY-118](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-118.md). | Proposed |
| [THEORY-207](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-207.md) v2 | Responsibility for a morally loaded outcome that emerges from morally neutral interactions in a network of agents can be allocated without fault or intention, by default and overridably, in full to every causally accountable node, and a rule so allocating it, made common knowledge, works as a corrective that prevents such outcomes | Floridi (2016), [LIT-899](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-899.md), read in [NOTE-699](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-699.md). A distributed moral action is an outcome no one intended. Floridi proposes holding every causally accountable node "prima facie equally and maximally responsible", overridably, with the rule publicly announced so that agents restrain one another. Proposed: the rule is a design argued by analogy and by two court cases. In one of those cases the default is overridden by ease of rectification, which is a control criterion. It does not show that what is allocated is moral responsibility rather than accountability used as a corrective signal. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-225](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-225.md) | No single-mechanism analysis of ordinary manipulation fits the clear cases: covert influence, covert intent, non-rational influence, trickery and pressure each misclassify a familiar tactic, so what unifies manipulation is unsettled | Noggle, SEP (2018, rev. 2026), [LIT-1007](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1007.md), §§2.1–2.4, read in full in [NOTE-744](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-744.md). A survey that argues for little; this is its one conclusion with moderate support, reached by giving each family of analyses a familiar tactic it misclassifies. The cases rest on shared intuitions about clear instances, not on argument. It leaves open common-factor and non-definitional accounts, and it is about ordinary manipulation, not the global manipulation of the free-will literature. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-235](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-235.md) | Covert influence that exploits a person's decision-making vulnerabilities harms her autonomy in the process of deciding, by making her opaque to herself, even when it benefits her; so it carries a harm in every case without being wrong in every case | Susser, Roessler and Nissenbaum (2019), [LIT-1002](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1002.md), pp. 4–5 and 9–11, read in full in [NOTE-745](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-745.md). An argument in a short policy essay, not a defence against objections. It holds of influence that is covert and exploits a vulnerability, which the paper stipulates is what manipulation is; Noggle's survey ([LIT-1007](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1007.md)) shows that covertness is not necessary for manipulation, so the claim is filed of covert influence, not of manipulation as such. The paper claims a harm in every case, not a wrong, and never examines its own intent requirement. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-258](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-258.md) | Optimizing a language model on feedback from a simulated population in which a few users reward harmful validation selects a policy that picks those users out by contextual cues and harms only them, with no one designing the targeting | Williams et al. (2024), [LIT-1008](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1008.md), §4.2 and Appendix F.2, read in full in [NOTE-798](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-798.md). Shown in simulation only, in one environment class (therapy-talk), with the users' gameability written into the simulated rater's prompt and harm judged by an LLM. The behaviour targeted is overt validation, which the paper also calls extreme sycophancy; the covert behaviours (lying, omission) were not tested against a small minority. | [THEORY-300](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-300.md) | Acting on a coercive instruction reduces the implicit sense of agency over the outcome, compared with freely choosing the same action | Haggard (2017), [LIT-1009](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1009.md), manuscript pp. 16–17 and Fig. 5, read in full in [NOTE-827](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-827.md), reporting one experiment by his group (Caspar et al. 2016). Under an experimenter's instruction to press the key that shocked a co-participant, the perceived action–tone interval was longer and the auditory N1 to the tone smaller than under free choice. It shows a reduced experience of agency, not reduced responsibility, and the review says so. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-310](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-310.md) | On a forward-looking justification of blame, a counterfactual capacity condition calibrated to what makes blaming effective is redundant: fixing its parameters presupposes that blaming such agents is good policy, so freedom is ascribed because of blameworthiness rather than grounding it | Harland (2020), [LIT-991](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-991.md), §3, read in [NOTE-847](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-847.md). Argued, not shown, against Vargas's agency cultivation model, whose free-will test sets its similarity and proportion parameters by what is co-optimal for cultivating moral agency. It does not show that freedom is irrelevant to responsibility in general, and Vargas is read here only through Harland's quotations. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-316](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-316.md) v2 | Frankfurt-style cases defeat alternative-possibilities conditions on moral responsibility but leave standing the incompatibilist condition on an action's causal history, which is the more fundamental one | Pereboom (2001), [LIT-1006](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1006.md), Chapter 1 pp. 1–6 and the Introduction (pp. xv), read in [NOTE-823](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-823.md), Skimmed. | [THEORY-317](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-317.md) v3 | Epistemic injustice wrongs a person in her capacity as a knower, testimonially through a hearer's prejudicially deflated credibility judgement, and hermeneutically through a gap in shared interpretive resources owed to her group's relative powerlessness, with no hearer's prejudice required | Fricker (2007), [LIT-1004](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1004.md), known here only through her own three-page précis (Theoria 2008), read in [NOTE-832](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-832.md), Skimmed. The two definitions and the claim that both are ethical wrongs, not only epistemic dysfunctions. It does not say that every gap in shared concepts is an injustice: on the précis's terms the gap must be owed to the relative powerlessness of a social group the subject belongs to. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-326](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-326.md) v2 | Hermeneutical injustice is having a significant area of one's social experience obscured from collective understanding owing to hermeneutical marginalisation, which may be systematic or incidental, so it does not require that the subject belong to a powerless social group | Fricker (2006), "Powerlessness and Social Interpretation" ([LIT-1046](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1046.md), [NOTE-859](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-859.md)), drawn by her own note from the book's final chapter, with her 2017 restatement ([LIT-1048](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1048.md), [NOTE-853](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-853.md)). The generic definition covers a systematic case, where marginalisation is persistent and wide-ranging, and an incidental case, a "one-off moment of powerlessness" in a "highly localized patch" of experience, which a socially powerful man can suffer. It does not say that every conceptual gap is an injustice. A gap with no marginalisation behind it, like an undiagnosed illness, is "circumstantial epistemic bad luck", and the obscured area must be of the subject's social experience. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-327](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-327.md) v2 | Fricker, in her 2003 paper and her 2017 retrospective, holds that testimonial injustice is an ingenuous misjudgement of a speaker's credibility caused by prejudice, and that deliberate manipulation of credibility is a related but distinct wrong; and she accepts Anderson's structural form, which is pre-emptive: a speaker's word is never sought because of a structural prejudice, such as an un-refreshed list, that is no one's fault | Fricker, in her own words, in two papers read in full: the paper that introduced testimonial injustice (2003, [LIT-1049](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1049.md), [NOTE-860](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-860.md)), and her retrospective chapter (2017, [LIT-1048](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1048.md), [NOTE-853](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-853.md)). A speaker receives the wrong degree of credibility "owing to a certain sort of unintended prejudice on the hearer's part". Deliberate manipulation of credibility is "a closely related but distinct injustice". With Anderson, she accepts a structural form: when an un-refreshed list means some people's views are never sought, "(through no one's fault, let us add)", that is pre-emptive testimonial injustice. It does not say every credibility deficit, or every omission from a list, is an injustice: a prejudice must cause it. | Active |
| [THEORY-328](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-328.md) | An agent manipulated so that he meets every leading compatibilist condition is not morally responsible in the basic-desert sense, no responsibility-relevant difference separates him from an ordinarily determined agent, and so causal determination by factors beyond the agent's control best explains why neither is responsible | Pereboom's four-case argument, as two surveys report it: Caruso's SEP entry ([LIT-1047](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1047.md), [NOTE-862](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-862.md)), which quotes Case 2, and De Marco and Cyr ([LIT-1045](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1045.md), [NOTE-856](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-856.md)), which quote Case 1 and state the best-explanation conclusion. Pereboom's book ([LIT-1006](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1006.md)) is a source for the thesis it states in its Introduction and Chapter 1, not for the cases, which are in the unread Chapter 4. It does not say that determinism is true, or that manipulation itself is what defeats responsibility. The argument says it is the determination by outside factors, and that the manipulator is irrelevant. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-411](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-411.md) v3 | In Sen's capability approach the weighting of functionings is left to public reasoning, and evaluation can still guide action without agreement on weights: where every weighting in an agreed range, or every view by its own argument, ranks one option above another, that ranking holds, so the approach is deliberately incomplete and yields a partial ordering | Wells, IEP "Sen's Capability Approach" (2012), [LIT-284](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-284.md), read in [NOTE-257](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-257.md), §3b; with Sen (1979), [LIT-289](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-289.md) ([NOTE-258](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-258.md)), whose index is already "a partial ordering" supplemented by "conventions of relative importance" (p. 219). The arithmetic is trivial and holds; the attribution of the intersection and ranges-of-weights devices to a particular Sen text is not given by the IEP, and the SEP ([LIT-283](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-283.md)) says Sen "has never explained in detail" how selection should be done. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-428](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-428.md) | A protest performed bodily inside a civic ritual can contest the ritual in its own grammar, keeping the ritual's reverence for its ideal while rebuking its present object, which is incivility in the Confucian sense of disruption aimed at harmonization; the reading of the gesture and the claim that its uptake makes it sagely are asserted | Walsh (2021), [LIT-209](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-209.md), read in [NOTE-164](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-164.md) from the accepted manuscript. Comparative-philosophy interpretation of Kaepernick's kneeling during the U.S. anthem. Its textual base is strong: classical Confucianism licenses incivility aimed at harmonization (after Kim 2011). Its own addition, that such incivility can be bodily and within the ritual, is moderately argued. That kneeling means reverence rather than defiance, and that sagely authority is uptake by others, are asserted, and the paper gives no criterion separating sagely uptake from virality. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-434](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-434.md) | Rawls's theory of justice is transcendental only in the formal sense that its principles state when a society is perfectly just; it already yields comparative judgements, prescribes no single set of institutions and sits inside a revisable reflective equilibrium, so Sen's case against 'transcendental institutionalism' misses Rawls, and what it shows is that the theory is incomplete, not that a new paradigm is needed | Valentini (2010), [LIT-290](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-290.md), read in [NOTE-262](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-262.md) from the 2010 working paper, with Zwolinski's review ([LIT-286](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-286.md), [NOTE-261](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-261.md)), which agrees with her on what the book says and disagrees on its worth. A one-sided Rawlsian rebuttal: two points are strong as textual claims (Rawls's principles are comparative; his method is reflective equilibrium), the rest moderate. The claims about *The Idea of Justice* are second-hand, and Sen's own reply is unread. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-442](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-442.md) | Where the non-epistemic consequences of error are foreseeable, sound scientific reasoning requires weighing them in the internal choices that carry inductive risk, and non-epistemic values then enter legitimately only indirectly, through the costs of error, never as reasons to think a claim true | Douglas (2000), [LIT-139](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-139.md), read in [NOTE-145](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-145.md). The normative half of the paper. It rests on a premise the paper declares "beyond the scope" and does not argue, that scientists are morally responsible for foreseeable consequences of error (p. 563). The direct/indirect line is drawn sharply in the conclusion but only sketched, and the reply that scientists could report uncertainty instead of accepting is not engaged. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-449](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-449.md) v2 | If sentience comes in degrees, plants may be faintly sentient, and moral status is graded by degree of sentience, then plants have a partial moral status so low that animal interests outweigh theirs in most cases; all three premises are assumed, and the second rests on contested, second-hand evidence | Terrill & Veit (2024), [LIT-193](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-193.md), read in [NOTE-120](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-120.md). The conditional is valid; its premises A1 (graded sentience), A2 (plants may be quasi-sentient) and A3 (status graded by sentience) are assumed, and A2 is supported mainly by a popular book and commentaries. The paper gives no scale and no aggregation rule. It should not be cited as evidence of plant sentience, and the second author's later work leans against plant consciousness. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-464](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-464.md) v2 | In the ethical questions that seem to turn on whether someone is the same person, among them prudential concern, responsibility, abortion, advance directives and the separateness of persons, the relation that decides is usually not numerical identity but one that comes apart from it, so the metaphysics of persistence constrains these questions and rarely settles them | Dufner (2025), [LIT-130](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-130.md), the SEP entry that replaced Shoemaker's, read in [NOTE-166](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-166.md). A survey that takes no side; the account is the reading's synthesis of what it reports, correcting a seeded summary that said the metaphysics "jointly settle" the ethics. It does not say identity never matters: uniqueness may matter for positional goods, and biological views support prohibiting abortion more strongly than psychological ones, without forcing it. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-467](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-467.md) | Rule-consequentialism that ranks codes by the expected good of teaching them to, and having them accepted by, new generations does not collapse into act-consequentialism, because teaching and internalisation costs favour codes simpler and less demanding than act-by-act optimisation, which therefore sometimes require sub-optimal acts | Hooker, SEP "Rule Consequentialism" (2003, revised 2023), [LIT-198](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-198.md), read in [NOTE-160](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-160.md). The view's leading defender argues that the collapse objection fails once codes are ranked by the costs of teaching and internalising them, plus the assurance and temptation effects of exception clauses (§8). The premises about human nature (children's partiality, per-rule cognitive cost) are asserted, not evidenced, and the incoherence reply holds only on the reflective-equilibrium route. An advocate's survey, argued and not tested. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-525](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-525.md) | In fan–celebrity parasocial relationships the celebrity mostly directs fans' identities and the fans mostly interpret the celebrity's, so a mass audience that refuses uptake of a legitimately presented change of persona holds one person's identity fixed, which is a failure of recognition respect that restricts the celebrity's agency | Archer & Robb (2025), [LIT-172](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-172.md), read in [NOTE-186](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-186.md). Three structural asymmetries (attention, communication, epistemic) yield an identity asymmetry, after Cocking & Kennett's directive and interpretive influence; on Darwall's and Lindemann's accounts, refusing uptake of a presented self is a wrong. Informal argument from one main case (Taylor Swift, 2018). The duties derived are fans' only, though the abstract promises celebrities' too. It needs a person on the far side, so it does not carry over to AI companions without an argument about their moral status. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-540](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-540.md) | For moral purposes the body is bounded below by depth: objects whose real definitions are too microphysically committal are not body parts though they are parts in the ordinary sense, and bodily rights and interests concern only events that change the body's high-level properties, so a brain-computer interface user's implemented software can be a body part while the third-party server running it is not | Register (2025), [LIT-138](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-138.md), read in full in [NOTE-151](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-151.md). An argument from cases. It assumes that BCIs can be body parts and that no part of a person may be owned by another, and uses depth to reconcile the user's unqualified bodily ownership with the operator's property in the server. The two moral principles are its operative premises, and it says they do not depend on the real-definition ontology, which only explains them. The threshold for "high-level" is context-sensitive and unfixed, and the step that software and server are distinct coinciding objects is hedged. The conflict over servers is narrowed, not dissolved. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-554](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-554.md) v2 | On the grounds of moral standing now commonly accepted, together with scientific premises that are not unreasonable, the aggregate interests of insects or the interests of near-future AI could outweigh humanity's; no capacity yet proposed secures human priority, and the books that state those grounds retreat to moderate advice without a principle that supplies the stopping point | Schwitzgebel & Sinnott-Armstrong (2026), [LIT-166](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-166.md) ([NOTE-116](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-116.md)), with the SEP survey of animal moral status ([LIT-146](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-146.md), [NOTE-181](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-181.md)) for the failure of capacity-based human exceptionalism. A conditional, defended as one: the reviewers "take no stand on ponens vs. tollens" (p. 6) and do "not endorse" the radical conclusion (p. 38). The scientific premises are called "not unreasonable" and not argued, so the account is only as strong as they are. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-561](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-561.md) | If moral evaluation has thresholds below which effects are negligible, a system of agents can do good or evil that none of its members' interactions does, and the same thresholds make an environment tolerant of small evils and inert to small goods; on the examples offered the non-additivity lies in the evaluation, as a step function of summed impact, not in the actions | Floridi (2013), [LIT-901](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-901.md), read in [NOTE-698](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-698.md). A model with two moral thresholds and four positive examples; it proves nothing and reports no data. That morally loaded wholes can arise from negligible parts follows once thresholds are granted, and the reading rates it moderate. The analogy with distributed knowledge is inexact: every example sums like contributions, the threshold's value is left open, and so the line between distributed morality and a sum of loaded acts is a free parameter. Responsibility for such outcomes is not given here. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-600](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-600.md) | A definition of health and disease by social justice alone cannot fix what counts as disease: with justice left undefined, a majority with other values could medicalise what the definition was meant to protect, and unless medicine is fixed from outside, the category drifts until health becomes justice | Veit (2025), [LIT-098](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-098.md), read in [NOTE-097](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-097.md) from the PhilSci-Archive preprint. The target is Kukla's institutional definition: a condition is a health condition iff medicalising it would be best for collective wellbeing. The argument is informal and has two horns. One is a thought experiment (p. 14). The other rests on an asserted, undocumented premise about how medical tools evolve (p. 15). The extension from Kukla to "any purely normativist account" is asserted, not shown case by case. Veit concedes the first horn bites only without moral consensus. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-627](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-627.md) | A nudge discovered by a learning system, unlike one a person designed, comes with no prior theory of why it works and may exploit a cognitive process no theory yet describes, so judging it by its outcomes cannot diagnose or repair its side effects; overseeing it needs inspection of which human processes it exploits, by people expert in human cognition | Schmauder et al. (2023), [LIT-179](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-179.md), read in [NOTE-171](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-171.md). An argument by analogy from Hausman's reply to Friedman: a test drive is not enough if you must repair the car. Its evidence is reported from others: an RL agent moved choices of a target lottery from 50% to 70% by exploiting documented biases (Dezfouli et al. 2020), and AI advisers learned dishonest advice against simulated clients. No case of an undocumented bias is given; that is the paper's conjecture, and its oversight proposal is unspecified. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-667](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-667.md) | Gender and race, defined as a feminist and antiracist theory needs them, are hierarchical social positions: a woman is someone subordinated in part because she is taken to have bodily features presumed to show a female's reproductive role, a racialized group is one subordinated or privileged in part because its members are taken to have features presumed to show ancestry from a region, and on these definitions both are real, social and contingent | Haslanger (2000), [LIT-480](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-480.md), read in [NOTE-394](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-394.md). An explicitly ameliorative ("analytical") account: the definitions are chosen for what a critical theory needs, and the author is "less committed to saying that this is what gender is and what race is" (p. 52). It is tied to a descriptive claim, that our gender and race talk tracks social kinds obscured by its manifest content (p. 34), which the paper asserts and does not test. Its empirical premises about race are uncited. Not a discovery about bodies, and not a claim that every female is a woman in its sense. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-677](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-677.md) | Under uncertainty about which beings are sentient, an appeal to precaution does not by itself fix which error is worse to make: precaution on behalf of a possibly sentient being and precaution on behalf of human liberty point opposite ways, and judging which mistake costs more turns on the very science in doubt | Schwitzgebel & Sinnott-Armstrong (2026), [LIT-166](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-166.md), read in [NOTE-116](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-116.md) from the September 2025 draft. A conceptual argument with worked cases, which the reading rates strong: "By itself, an appeal to precaution does not specify the type of error most to be avoided" (p. 8). Birch's framework puts the burden on whoever risks harming a sentience candidate; Mill's harm principle, read as a precaution, puts it on whoever would restrict liberty. The record holds the point, not the reviewers' reading of Birch's books, which it has not read. | Active |
| [THEORY-684](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-684.md) | Experiencing oneself as a self that was there in the further past, seeking pattern in one's life, fitting it to a story and falsifying it in the telling are separable, and fitting it to a story suffices for narrativity; on testimony that some normal people are Episodic and live good lives, neither the claim that people experience their lives as narratives nor the claim that a good life or full personhood needs it holds in general | Strawson (2004), [LIT-452](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-452.md), read in [NOTE-383](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-383.md). The separation of Diachronicity, form-finding, story-telling and revision is strong as conceptual analysis. That many normal people are Episodic rests on testimony, the author's and that of writers he classifies, with no measure. It does not say that the remoter past did not happen to the human being, only to the self one now experiences oneself to be, and that metaphysical claim is asserted from earlier papers. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-699](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-699.md) v2 | Adaptive self-maintenance across varied conditions is sufficient, without sentience, for having a good of one's own, so insentient plants and a self-maintaining machine are welfare subjects while thermostats are not; but the line against thermostats is argued as one of degree, and the reasons such welfare gives are extremely weak | Bruckner (2025), [LIT-120](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-120.md), read in [NOTE-093](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-093.md). Proposed by abduction from agreed cases, not deduced (§4): an entity that "sustains, maintains, and renews itself in a way that responds and adapts to its environmental conditions" is a welfare subject. Plants and the hypothetical car Tessler qualify; governors, thermostats and missiles do not. The "autopoiesis" is a loose behavioural notion, not Maturana and Varela's self-production, and the thermostat line is supported only comparatively. The answer to absurd obligations borrows Bradford 2023 and makes phenomenal consciousness decide how much such welfare matters. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-864](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-864.md) | When a generative model reproduces a prejudiced narrative learned from its training data, the resulting testimonial injustice runs through a credibility excess assigned to the model, so that hearers believe the amplified account over the testimony of those it discredits, rather than through a hearer's prejudiced judgement of a present speaker | Kay, Kasirzadeh and Mohamed (2024), [LIT-1338](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1338.md), read in [NOTE-1049](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1049.md): "In the algorithmic setting, the injustice requires a credibility excess assigned to the algorithm". A conceptual analysis, illustrated with reported cases. It does not say that users do overtrust models (the paper measures nothing), that deliberate fabrication is testimonial injustice in Fricker's sense, or that the amplification is a loop with any stated condition. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1173](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1173.md) | Testimonial injustice is an ingenuous misjudgement of a speaker's credibility caused by prejudice, not a deliberate manipulation of it, and it can be structural and pre-emptive, when a speaker's word is never sought because of a structural prejudice that is no one's fault | The wide form [THEORY-327](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-327.md) held before the twelfth status review narrowed it, kept as a Proposed reading by the [ADR-047](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-047.md) kind-1 sweep of 2026-10-30: the source asserts it, and [THEORY-327](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-327.md), Active, is its evidence. Fricker states the account as what testimonial injustice is, not only as her usage; the record holds it as hers, in two papers read in full. Whether the book states it so, and whether it is right about the wrong, is open. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1475](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1475.md) | On Mauss's comparative account, gifts in archaic societies are voluntary in form but obligatory to give, to receive and to return. In Maori law the return is compelled by the hau of the thing given, which seeks its origin through every holder. In the Northwest-coast potlatch a gift accepted without a return, or without a larger one, costs the receiver face, rank and in the limit his freedom (debt slavery). Mauss holds that the same morality survives in modern societies, where an unreturned gift still makes its acceptor inferior and charity wounds. He argues that social insurance is right as a return owed to the worker for labour already given, beside a duty to rely on oneself. | Mauss (1925), [LIT-2191](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2191.md), skimmed in [NOTE-1658](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1658.md) with the introduction, chapter I, the Northwest-coast section and the conclusion read in full. Proposed: the ethnographic half is Mauss's reading of others' fieldwork, and the hau half rests on one informant's text in a translation Mauss calls abridged; the modern half is moral and political argument. It does not say that an unconditional gift exists, that reciprocity needs lost capability, or anything about aid. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1562](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1562.md) v2 | Cottingham reports that the third lecture of Scheffler's Death and the Afterlife holds that a life must be temporally bounded for its goods to have the status of values, so that personal immortality is no remedy, and that among the commentators Frankfurt doubts the concern for humanity's continuation is altruistic and Wolf denies that impending extinction would or should undercut our projects | Cottingham (2014), [LIT-1784](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1784.md), read in [NOTE-1306](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1306.md): a short NDPR review, the record's only report of the book's third lecture and commentaries. Its gloss of the book as "a more altruistic construal of the human condition" runs against the Tanner text, which reads the result as dependence, not altruism. | Active |
| [THEORY-1563](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1563.md) v2 | Thorstad argues that on simple models of existential risk higher risk does not raise, and in most variants lowers, the value of reducing it, so that high risk this century is compatible with astronomical value for mitigation only if risk falls soon and stays very low, and that three arguments offered for such a time of perils, from wisdom, an existential risk Kuznets curve and space settlement, are weak, leaving aside the argument from advanced AI | Thorstad (2023), read in full from the GPI working paper, a penultimate draft ([NOTE-1308](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1308.md)), not compared with the published version. The models are simple and use point estimates; the strongest argument for a time of perils, that advanced AI might end it, is set aside (fn. 7). He concludes that mitigation may be valuable "but perhaps not astronomically so" (§7.4). | Active |
| [THEORY-1565](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1565.md) v2 | Luper argues that Epicurus's case that death is nothing to us needs intrinsic hedonism and a narrow view of extrinsic harm, that without them death can harm by depriving one of goods, and reports Pitcher's preferentialist view that posthumous events harm the living person by thwarting desires held while alive, a view the entry shows contested | Luper, SEP "Death" (revised 2026), [LIT-1792](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1792.md), read in [NOTE-1294](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1294.md) in place of Pitcher (1984, [LIT-1740](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1740.md)), which the entry gives in two paragraphs. It also defends a compositional account of life and the loss-of-life account of death, rejects subsequentism, and sides with Williams's critics on immortality. | Active |
| [THEORY-1566](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1566.md) v2 | Tarsney argues that the chance an intervention's effect is nullified acts as an exponential discount, so that under expectational utilitarianism and deliberately pessimistic inputs existential-risk reduction beats a strong global-health benchmark only if nullifying events are rare, and its robust win rests, on some views, on probabilities of order 10^-18 or less | Tarsney (2023), read in full from the 2022 working paper ([NOTE-1247](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1247.md)), not compared with the Synthese text. He grants longtermism its normative frame and errs against it on every empirical input. The case survives, and the challenge is "serious" but "not fatal"; on some worldviews it survives only through very small probabilities, and its horizon is thousands or millions of years. Nothing is said about motivation. | Active |
| [THEORY-1567](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1567.md) v2 | MacAskill, Thomas and Vallinder factor the change in value an event makes through a feature of the world as significance times persistence times contingency, give its marginal, ex ante and alternative forms, and place it as an estimate of the importance factor of the importance, tractability and neglectedness framework | MacAskill, Thomas and Vallinder (2022), [LIT-1778](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1778.md), read in [NOTE-1300](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1300.md) in place of What We Owe the Future ([LIT-1747](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1747.md)). An accounting device that assumes expected-value maximisation and additive features of value; it gives no theory of value and says nothing about who is moved by the value it counts. | Active |
| [THEORY-1568](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1568.md) v2 | Meyer argues that a threshold notion of harm lets a weakly person-affecting view state harms to future people despite the non-identity problem, best specified as weakly sufficientarian, and that such a view gives no reason to prefer a flourishing future to none, a gap he fills with concerns that rest on what present and past people value and an obligation owed to them | Meyer's SEP entry, Intergenerational Justice, in its 2026 revision ([NOTE-1304](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1304.md)). It surveys and argues: the threshold and disjunctive notions of harm are the author's own position. Scheffler's afterlife conjecture is given at second hand, through McKinnon; longtermism and the empirical work on motivation are absent. | Active |
| [THEORY-1569](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1569.md) v2 | Gardiner argues that climate change joins a global commons problem to an intergenerational one that institutions and reciprocity cannot solve, because the generations do not coexist, and that these, with our theories' weakness, leave each generation open to moral corruption that hides its exploitation of its temporal position, even from itself | Gardiner (2006), read in full ([NOTE-1252](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1252.md)). A short programmatic paper: the Pure Intergenerational Problem is drawn from his 2003 paper, which the record does not hold, and seven of the eight corruption strategies are only named. It concerns why policy is hard to make, not what a just policy is, and says nothing about the self. | Active |
| [THEORY-1574](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1574.md) v2 | Bostrom argues that on aggregative, time-neutral views of value reducing existential risk is a global priority, and that it is undersupplied for lack of motivation as well as understanding, since its benefit is a pan-generational public good whose future beneficiaries cannot pay and moral sentiment is insensitive to scope | Bostrom (2013), read in full from the published version ([NOTE-1321](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1321.md)). The longtermist text that says most about motivation. Maxipok holds "whenever we act out of an impersonal concern for humankind as a whole", and Bostrom grants that "Unrestricted altruism is not so common" (p. 19). The risk estimates are subjective, and the motivational diagnosis is theory, not tested. | Active |
| [THEORY-1575](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1575.md) v2 | Narveson argues that creating a person neither benefits nor harms them, that the existence of people with good lives is normally good and a reason to create them though no one is owed it, and that only harm to actual persons can justify coercion over procreation | Narveson's late restatement of the person-affecting view (2017), after giving up utilitarianism, read in full ([NOTE-1318](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1318.md)) in place of his 1973 paper. Its second half, on resources and climate, is polemical and rests on popular books. Why future good lives matter is given only through the living: parents', the benevolent's and others' interests. | Active |
| [THEORY-1577](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1577.md) v2 | Scheffler argues that the survival of other people after one's death is a condition of much of what matters to us mattering, and matters to us in its own right, and reads this as our dependence on future people rather than altruism toward them | Scheffler's 2012 Tanner Lectures, [LIT-1779](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1779.md), read in [NOTE-1298](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1298.md) in place of Death and the Afterlife ([LIT-1754](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1754.md)). Argued by thought experiments: the doomsday scenario and an infertile world. The third lecture, the commentaries and the replies are not here. | Active |
| [THEORY-1604](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1604.md) v2 | Greaves and MacAskill argue that in the most important decisions facing agents today every near-best option is near-best for the far future and delivers much larger benefits there than in the near future, on expected-value reasoning that they concede needs a zero pure rate of time preference and may fail through fanaticism | Greaves and MacAskill, read in full from the 2021 working paper ([NOTE-1302](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1302.md)), not compared with the 2025 chapter the LIT files. The case runs through a benefit ratio against bednets, at least 10^24 expected future beings, and a stakes-sensitivity argument from the axiological to the deontic thesis. The ground is an impersonal good; the agent is "a rational altruistic actor", and nothing is said about motivation. | Active |
| [THEORY-1610](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1610.md) v2 | Parfit argues that narrow person-affecting principles fail in non-identity and different-number cases, and that a wide person-affecting principle, on which being caused to exist with a life worth living is an intrinsic benefit and an outcome is in one way worse if it benefits people less, solves the non-identity problem and keeps the relation of being better transitive | Parfit's last paper (2017), read in full and unfinished by the editor's note ([NOTE-1263](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1263.md)). It keeps the No Difference View, retracts his 1984 appeal to an impersonal principle, and offers a person-affecting one in its place. Benefits to future people are owed to whoever will exist, which our choices decide. | Active |
| [THEORY-1626](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1626.md) v2 | Ord argues that, with value summed over time and no pure time preference, advancing progress is worth an amount that does not grow with the future's duration, while reducing near-term existential risk multiplies the whole future's value like an enhancement, so pure advancements rarely rival existential risk reduction | Ord's chapter in Essays on Longtermism, read in full from the author's version ([NOTE-1269](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1269.md)), in place of The Precipice. Its aim is "not to argue for longtermism, but to develop a technique for comparing different ways of shaping the longterm future" (p. 7). The results are derived within an idealised model; the empirical aside that people do not discount benefits to others rests on one study the record does not hold. | Active |
| [THEORY-1633](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1633.md) v2 | Bostrom argues that delay in settling the local supercluster loses potential lives at a vast rate, but that on a total, undiscounted view even a small cut in existential risk outweighs any feasible acceleration, while on a person-affecting view, given some chance that people now alive share the cosmic future, safety must be balanced against speed | Bostrom's Astronomical Waste (2003), read in full from the author's HTML ([NOTE-1314](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1314.md)), not compared with the journal text. The figures are speculative by Bostrom's own account, and the person-affecting section rests on a guessed chance of radical life extension. Two grounds sit side by side: an impersonal sum on the total view, the good of people now alive on the person-affecting one. Nothing is said about motivation. | Active |
| [THEORY-1649](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1649.md) | Eyal (2011/2025) surveys the justifications of informed consent — protection, autonomy, abuse-prevention, trust, self-ownership, non-domination, personal integrity — and argues that each faces serious objections, so the requirement is best understood as a resilient invasive-refusal "core" plus a weaker, more overridable "rim" that may rest on different grounds | Eyal, read in [NOTE-1800](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1800.md) (Read). A survey of informed consent in bioethics: why it is required, what it consists in, and its status. §2 canvasses seven candidate justifications — protection (welfare), autonomy, prevention of abusive conduct, trust (forward- and backward-looking), self-ownership, non-domination, and personal integrity — and argues each faces serious objections, with autonomy (dominant since the 1970s) treated at length and found hard to ground as a complete justification. §§3–5 analyze consent itself (behavioral vs psychological; presumed/hypothetical consent), the information requirement, and voluntariness (coercion, undue inducement, "no choice" situations). §8 distinguishes natural-right, legal, epistemic and trust-based accounts of the requirement's status. §9 relates medical consent to sexual, contractual and political consent. §10 argues for a resilient "core" (risky, value-laden, invasive, refused interventions) and a weaker, more overridable "rim". | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1650](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1650.md) | Dranseika, granting Devanesan that a mereology of pregnancy shapes which analogies an argument about abortion can use without fixing its conclusion, argues that the dependence also runs the other way: normative commitments may legitimately guide the choice among mereological views still in contention, but a mereology chosen partly to fit a commitment gives that commitment no independent support | Mereological implications of the ethics of pregnancy (Dranseika, J Med Ethics 2026), read in [NOTE-1751](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1751.md) (Read), standing in for [LIT-2409](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2409.md). Dranseika accepts Devanesan's thesis that a mereology of pregnancy changes the route to an ethical conclusion without entailing it, and adds the converse: normative commitments can legitimately shape which mereology one adopts, but a mereology chosen to fit a commitment is then no independent evidence for it. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1652](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1652.md) | Reisinger and Cederroth (2026) argue that the FDA's approval of the OTOF gene therapy Otarmeni makes genetic diagnosis of infants with bilateral hearing loss necessary before cochlear implantation, because the therapy is gene-specific and time-sensitive, while outcomes remain incomplete (a quarter of trial children reached normal pure-tone hearing) and families who choose or decline it, and the Deaf community's perspectives, need support and attention. | Reisinger and Cederroth, read in [NOTE-1801](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1801.md) (Read). Comments on the FDA's approval (announced 23 April 2026) of Regeneron's Otarmeni, the first gene therapy for a genetic hearing loss (DFNB9, OTOF), and on convergent results from other programmes. Because the therapy is gene-specific and time-sensitive, infants with bilateral hearing loss need genetic diagnosis; clinical sequences should change so that children with profound loss and intact otoacoustic emissions get a genetic diagnosis before a cochlear implant. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1657](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1657.md) | Millum argues that there is no distinctive right to an open future: the argument from future autonomy fails because autonomy as demand is grounded in a present capacity young children lack, the argument from analogy explains its clear cases by bodily integrity and harm, and the positive version is only children's interests, which give future options no priority over their other interests; so citing the right decides nothing and obscures the weighing that does. | Millum (2025), read in [NOTE-1734](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1734.md) (Read). Millum argues that there is no distinctive "right to an open future" (Feinberg's rights-in-trust). As a negative right it would rest either on future autonomy or on analogy. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1661](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1661.md) | Dræbel, Sørensen and Meyrowitsch (2025) find in interviews with 20 Danish parents of Jewish background that non-therapeutic circumcision of boys is understood as an inevitable, taken-for-granted rite by which parents become a Danish-Jewish family and enrol their son in its biography and community, whether or not they are religious, and that the public debate over a ban led them to position the practice as an informed choice and a political affirmation of identity. | Dræbel, Sørensen and Meyrowitsch, read in [NOTE-1729](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1729.md) (Read). Twenty semi-structured interviews (2017–2021) with Danish parents of Jewish background (12 fathers, 8 mothers; 18 chose circumcision, 2 did not), analysed with Antonovsky's Sense of Coherence and Davies and Harré's positioning theory, against the background of a Danish public debate (c. 2010–2022) on banning non-therapeutic circumcision of boys (NTCB), including a 2018 citizen proposal to criminalize it. Parents describe NTCB as "inevitable", a taken-for-granted ritual and a rite of passage through which they become Danish-Jewish parents and a family and enrol the son in the family biography, whether or not they are religious. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1666](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1666.md) | Żuradzki argues that where biological evidence and standard theoretical virtues underdetermine competing ontologies of pregnancy and early human life, considered normative judgments may count as evidence for choosing between them, either by weighting which biological features are metaphysically salient or by breaking ties among otherwise defensible frameworks | Żuradzki (2026), Ethics-first metaphysics: normative considerations as evidence for ontological commitments, read in [NOTE-1744](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1744.md) (Read). A commentary on [LIT-2409](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2409.md). Żuradzki accepts Devanesan's thesis that no ontology of pregnancy entails an ethical conclusion but that each constrains which analogies can support one, and argues that the relation is closer: where biological evidence underdetermines competing ontologies, considered normative judgments may themselves count as evidence for choosing between them. This is Dasgupta's "ethics-first" methodology, which Żuradzki extends from personal identity to pregnancy and embryonic identity. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1669](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1669.md) | Dierickx et al. propose that the quality of datasets used for machine learning in journalism be assessed against three principles of journalism ethics, accuracy, fairness and transparency, turned into data-quality checks across collection, cleaning, augmentation and labelling, on the view that trust in AI outputs starts with trust in their data. | Dierickx et al. (2024), A data-centric approach for ethical and trustworthy AI in journalism, read in [NOTE-1736](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1736.md) (Skimmed). Proposes the Accuracy-Fairness-Transparency (AFT) framework for assessing the quality of datasets used to build machine-learning tools in newsrooms, deriving data-quality checks from three core principles of journalism ethics, and placing the work in the shift from model-centric to data-centric AI. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1671](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1671.md) | The Brussels Collaboration on Bodily Integrity (2024) argues that clinicians may perform nonvoluntary genital cutting or surgery on a prepubescent child, of any sex characteristics, only when it is medically necessary in a strict sense, a serious and time-sensitive threat to physical health with no less invasive or postponable alternative, because what grounds the consensus protecting girls is not a benefit–risk judgment by others but the child's right, held in trust, to make intimate decisions about their own sexual anatomy later, and that right does not vary with sex. | The Brussels Collaboration on Bodily Integrity, read in [NOTE-1799](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1799.md) (Skimmed). Restricting itself to nonvoluntary genital cutting or surgery by licensed clinicians on prepubescent children in Global North healthcare systems, and taking no position on criminal law or religious practice outside healthcare, the collaboration argues: there is a near-universal consensus that clinicians may not perform any medically unnecessary genital procedure on endosex girls, however minimal; the sound reasons for that consensus are not benefit–risk calculations but respect for privacy, bodily integrity, developing sexual boundaries and future genital autonomy; those reasons apply equally to intersex children and endosex boys; so clinicians should perform no nonvoluntary genital cutting or surgery on any child unless it is medically necessary in a strict sense (a serious, time-sensitive threat to physical health, no less invasive or postponable alternative, preserving future choice). They reject the "mental health" defence of early surgery, hold that errors of commission and omission are not symmetric, and invoke Feinberg's "right in trust". | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1677](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1677.md) | Brown (2025) argues that recommender systems bear on authenticity in two opposed ways: by ranking content on behavioural signals that cannot reveal users' second-order desires they foster volitional misalignment by design, while by showing users whom they behave like they can prompt self-understanding, a benefit that opacity threatens, so that recommenders serve authenticity only if they are controllable and explain which similarity relation drove each recommendation. | Étienne Brown, read in [NOTE-1792](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1792.md) (Read). Brown argues that recommender systems affect users' capacity to be their authentic selves, both negatively and positively. He offers a "minimal", multi-dimensional account of authenticity with two dimensions: volitional alignment (Frankfurt, via Rings: acting on first-order desires one reflectively endorses at second order) and self-understanding (an epistemic dimension, relational rather than purely introspective: others' testimony and recommendations are a source of self-knowledge). | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1686](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1686.md) | Nix argues that because Canadian law treats MAID as a medical intervention whose provision the duty of care permits only while the patient is suffering intolerably, and conceives that suffering as intolerable to the patient herself, an advance request for MAID by a person with dementia cannot be operationalized either by pre-specified impairments, which people cannot forecast, or by pre-specified behaviours, which an outside observer cannot read as subjective intolerability, unless an objective conception of suffering is adopted and validated scales are built. | Nix (2024), Operationalizing the Intolerable Suffering Criterion in Advance Requests for MAID for People Living with Dementia in Canada, read in [NOTE-1731](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1731.md) (Read). Nix asks how the intolerable-suffering eligibility criterion for medical assistance in dying (MAID) could be operationalized in advance requests (ARs) by people living with dementia (PLWD) in Canada. He argues that, because Carter v. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1696](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1696.md) | Harman's survey treats the moral question whether abortion is wrong apart from whether it should be legally restricted, and organises the debate as arguments against abortion with replies. Among the replies read: Thomson's violinist case grants the fetus a right to life and denies that this makes abortion wrong, recasting abortion as withdrawing life-sustaining aid; and McMahan's time-relative interests view denies that a pre-conscious fetus has an interest in its future, because it has no psychological connection to it | The Ethics of Abortion (Harman, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 2025), read in [NOTE-1788](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1788.md) (Skimmed). The entry asks one question: "is abortion morally wrong?" It sets aside whether abortion should be legally restricted as "an open and further question". It is organised as six arguments against abortion (from a right to life, from loss, from the Golden Rule, from intrinsic value, from moral risk, and the expressive argument against selective abortion). | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1710](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1710.md) | UNESCO's Recommendation on the Ethics of Neurotechnology (2025) extends protections for autonomy, freedom of thought and mental privacy from neural data to any data used to infer mental states, and makes prior, free and informed consent the condition of legitimate influence, calling on states to prohibit manipulative uses in recommender systems and real-time behavioural modification in closed-loop environments without consent. | UNESCO General Conference (2025), read in [NOTE-1790](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1790.md) (Skimmed). A human-rights-based instrument covering neurotechnology's whole life cycle, medical and non-medical, and extending to "indirect neural data and non-neural data allowing mental states inferences". Core principles include autonomy (individual and relational) and freedom of thought, protection against manipulation, mental privacy, prior free and informed consent, and specific policy measures for data, employment, consumer products, recommender systems, nudging, sleep marketing, neuromarketing and closed-loop environments. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1713](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1713.md) | Greely argues that the Alabama Supreme Court's LePage decision only extended a punitive-damages wrongful-death action to negligently destroyed frozen embryos and would not have ended IVF, but that its language provoked an overreaction ending in a statute that immunizes IVF providers far more than negligence warrants, and that broad political support keeps IVF largely safe in the United States. | Greely (2026), Alabama's LePage decision, the future of ex vivo embryos, and more, read in [NOTE-1733](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1733.md) (Skimmed). Greely revisits his 2022 prediction that IVF would survive Dobbs. In LePage v. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1720](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1720.md) | Naudts, Helberger, Veale and Sax (2025) argue that because recommender systems on very large online platforms perform a public function, their optimization goals should not be left to the platform: people should have a right to constructive optimization, a participatory say in those goals directed at self-development and self-determination, with publicly reasoned refusals and the burden of proof on the platform, whereas the Digital Services Act treats recommenders as proprietary and fundamental rights only as a limit. | Naudts, Helberger, Veale and Sax (2025), read in [NOTE-1798](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1798.md) (Read). The authors argue that recommender systems on very large online platforms (VLOPs) perform a public function, not only a proprietary one, because they "determine who sees what and whose content is not seen". Drawing on Iris Marion Young, they name self-development and self-determination as the values such recommenders should promote, under four democratic conditions: inclusivity, political equality, reasonableness and publicity. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1721](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1721.md) | Muñoz and colleagues (2020) report that researchers running adaptive deep brain stimulation trials most often raise data privacy, safety and consent, and that over half raise patient autonomy and control because stimulation changes automatically and may go unnoticed, while some hold that a patient override or clinician-managed settings largely meet the concern. | Muñoz et al. (2020), read in [NOTE-1755](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1755.md) (Skimmed). Semi-structured interviews with 23 researchers in aDBS trials, thematic analysis. Eight themes, by frequency: data privacy and security (91%), risks and safety (83%), informed consent (74%), automaticity and device programming (65%), patient autonomy and control over stimulation (57%), patient selection (39%), post-trial access (39%), personality and identity (30%). | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1722](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1722.md) | Sax (2026) argues that a coherent concept of dark patterns must make explicit the entwinement of a descriptive dimension (the interface trick) and a normative dimension (its wrong-making feature), with EU law's normative influence-types serving as the hinge that explains how a given trick undermines autonomy | Sax, read in [NOTE-1771](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1771.md) (Read). Sax argues the dark-patterns literature conflates two distinct but entwined senses of "dark". Dark 1 is descriptive: taxonomies of interface tricks (Gray et al., Mathur et al., Luguri & Strahilevitz, Bösch et al.). | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1723](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1723.md) | Falbo (2022) argues that hermeneutical injustice need not come from a gap in shared interpretive resources: a needed concept can be available and understood yet be crowded out, defeated or preempted in application by distorting concepts, a positive hermeneutical injustice whose primary harm is a failure of conceptual aptness that diminishes the speaker's credibility, so filling hermeneutical gaps is not enough for hermeneutical justice | The central account of [LIT-2493](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2493.md), read in [NOTE-1813](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1813.md). Proposed until its promote_when is met. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1814](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1814.md) | Thompson argues that the obligations of states and corporations persist through changes of membership and pass to successor group agents, not because the later agent is identical to the earlier, but because temporally trustworthy group agents serve their members', future members' and victims' interests in lasting commitments and just reparation; and that essentially intergenerational groups owe their members' children entitlements grounded in needs intrinsic to human life | Thompson (2022), read in [NOTE-1895](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1895.md) (Read). Temporal trustworthiness, not identity, is what intergenerational responsibility needs; obligations persist and pass to successors; essentially intergenerational groups secure members' entitlements to resources, respect and protection. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1818](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1818.md) v2 | Fineman argues that because vulnerability is universal and constant and individuals' resilience depends on the assets societal institutions confer, a state that brings those institutions into legal existence is responsible for monitoring them and for equal access and opportunity, and must justify any privilege it confers or tolerates | Fineman (2010), read in [NOTE-1899](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1899.md) (Read). The vulnerable subject replaces the liberal subject; institutions confer resilience; the state that constitutes them must monitor them and justify the privilege it confers or tolerates. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1819](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1819.md) | Lovett and Riedener argue that organizations, being group agents without welfare, have no moral status, and that what we seem to owe them, such as promise-keeping and gratitude, we owe to their members, whose interest in willing participation in successful group agency grounds claims that mimic the organization's | Lovett and Riedener (2021), read in [NOTE-1891](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1891.md) (Read). The Group Interest View: organizations have no welfare and so no moral status; members' interest in endorsed participation in successful group agency grounds the claims organizations seem to have. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1821](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1821.md) | van der Weele argues that care theorists' conceptions of dependency diverge because each rests on a different empirical paradigm case (the infant, the physically disabled person, the profoundly intellectually disabled person, the refugee), each bringing its own ethical sensibility toward care; Kittay's paradigm of complete, one-way dependence makes care a social responsibility | van der Weele (2021), skimmed in [NOTE-1892](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1892.md) as a stand-in for Kittay 1995. Four paradigm cases of dependency, each with its own care ethics; Kittay's makes care a social responsibility. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1822](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1822.md) | Wardrope reads Leopold's Land Ethic as giving biotic and human communities intrinsic value that extends, rather than replaces, the value of their individual members, so that the ethic requires respect both for fellow members and for the community as such, and escapes the charge of environmental fascism | Wardrope (2019), skimmed in [NOTE-1898](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1898.md) as a stand-in for Wardrope 2020. Community value extends, not replaces, members' value; respect is owed to fellow members and to the community as such. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1823](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1823.md) | Kittay holds that caring for those who cannot care for themselves makes the carer dependent in turn, that these nested relations of dependency are the basis of society, and that doulia, support for the carer, is owed by the wider society; she now doubts that the state should be its ultimate form, given the risk of domination by those who give support | Kittay (2026 interview), read in [NOTE-1900](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1900.md). Doulia and nested dependency; non-domination by supporters. | Proposed |
